diagnosis: Cerebral toxoplasmosis with focal seizures in advanced HIV

examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential diagnosis for this man's presentation, and what specifically points you toward each option.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Given a focal-onset seizure with secondary generalisation, preceding headache/fever and a progressive focal deficit in a man with CD4 48, my leading differential is cerebral toxoplasmosis — supported by multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white junction/basal ganglia and positive Toxoplasma IgG. Tuberculoma is next given the HIV/TB burden here, though sputum GeneXpert is negative and there's no TB contact. Primary CNS lymphoma is possible at this CD4 but usually presents as a single larger periventricular lesion. Neurocysticercosis is the leading cause of adult-onset seizures in South Africa generally but the lesion pattern and profound immunosuppression make it less likely here. Cryptococcoma is possible but usually presents with more meningitic features.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks: ranked list with reasoning linking CD4, lesion pattern/location, and serology to each diagnosis. Partial credit for an unranked or unjustified list.

examinerBank.question: Explain the pathophysiology of why this man developed a focal seizure that became generalised.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Reactivated Toxoplasma tachyzoites cause necrotising encephalitis with surrounding vasogenic oedema at the grey-white junction/basal ganglia. This creates an irritable, disorganised cortical focus that generates abnormal hypersynchronous electrical discharge — beginning focally in the cortical area controlling the right arm — before propagating across the corpus callosum and subcortical pathways to involve the whole cortex, producing secondary generalisation.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants mechanism: necrotising lesion → cortical irritability → focal discharge → propagation to generalised. Simply restating 'seizure' scores no marks.

examinerBank.question: Your patient continues to have rhythmic jerking of the right arm 6 minutes after arrival, with no improvement. What do you do, and why is timing important?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: This meets the t1 timepoint for generalised convulsive status epilepticus (5 minutes) — I would give IV lorazepam (or diazepam) immediately, or buccal/IM midazolam if no IV access, while checking glucose and electrolytes. Timing matters because GABA-A receptors progressively internalise and NMDA receptors upregulate at the synaptic membrane the longer a seizure continues, making benzodiazepines progressively less effective — so early treatment is critical to avoid needing second-line/anaesthetic agents.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Must state the 5-minute t1 threshold explicitly and explain benzodiazepine treatment-resistance mechanism for full marks.

examinerBank.question: Why would you avoid starting carbamazepine or phenytoin in this patient, even though they're effective antiseizure drugs?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, and phenobarbitone are potent hepatic enzyme inducers (CYP3A4) that significantly reduce plasma levels of dolutegravir, efavirenz, protease inhibitors, and rifampicin — risking ART/TB treatment failure and resistance. I would instead choose levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or valproate (with caution regarding teratogenicity in women of childbearing potential), none of which have this clinically significant interaction.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: High-yield, explicitly flagged local point — must name the enzyme induction mechanism and specific ART/TB drugs affected, not just 'they interact'.

examinerBank.question: His serum lactate was 3.1 mmol/L drawn 30 minutes after the witnessed convulsion. How does this help confirm this was a true seizure rather than syncope or a psychogenic event?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Serum lactate rises markedly after a true generalised tonic-clonic seizure due to the intense anaerobic muscular activity during the convulsion, and characteristically normalises within about an hour. A raised lactate shortly after the event supports a true convulsion; a normal lactate drawn soon afterward would argue against one. This, combined with cyanosis during the event, lateral tongue laceration, and prolonged post-ictal confusion, collectively supports a genuine epileptic seizure over syncope or PNES.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the timing-dependent physiology (rises then normalises by ~1 hour) and its use as a discriminator, not just 'lactate was raised so it was a seizure'.

framework: new-onset seizure: transient event characterisation → seizure vs mimic → provoked vs unprovoked → focal vs generalised onset → screen for structural/infective cause → ILAE epilepsy criteria → safety/driving/ART interactions

patient.name: Sibusiso Ngcobo
patient.personality: stoic, slow to volunteer information, embarrassed about his HIV status and reluctant to admit he defaulted his ART
patient.openingLine: Doctor... my family says my arm was shaking and I couldn't answer them. I don't remember it.

presentingComplaint: witnessed episode of right arm jerking with brief loss of awareness, referred by family after collapse at home

history.fact: Family says the episode started with his right hand and arm jerking rhythmically for about 2 minutes before he lost awareness and the whole body stiffened and jerked for another minute
His sister witnessed the event; she can be phoned — she says his lips went blue-grey during the shaking and he bit the side of his tongue
After the shaking stopped he was confused and drowsy for about 40 minutes, then slept for an hour; did not immediately know where he was
He was incontinent of urine during the episode, noticed by his sister
No warning before the episode — no strange smell, no rising stomach feeling, no déjà vu that he recalls
Headache and low-grade fevers for the past 10 days, worse in the mornings, plus increasing clumsiness of the right hand for about a week before the seizure
No previous seizures or funny turns ever before this
Diagnosed HIV positive 6 years ago; started on ART but stopped taking his tablets about 8 months ago after he changed jobs and moved suburbs, embarrassed to say he never went back to clinic
No known TB contact, no chronic cough, no night sweats besides the recent fevers, never treated for TB before
No prior hospital admissions, no head injury with loss of consciousness, no history of stroke or high blood pressure
Not on any current medication since defaulting ART; occasionally uses traditional muti from a local healer for the headaches
Drinks alcohol occasionally on weekends, denies smoking or recreational drug use; lives in Umlazi with his sister and her children
No family history of epilepsy or seizure disorders; father has hypertension
No visual disturbance, no neck stiffness noticed by him, no vomiting, no weight loss he's aware of, no rash

examination.general: Thin man, mildly unwell-looking, oriented but slow to respond, mild oral thrush noted. No neurocutaneous stigmata. No lymphadenopathy.
examination.respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no crackles, no bronchial breathing
examination.cardio: Normal heart sounds, no murmurs, JVP not raised
examination.neuro: GCS 15 but slow processing. Right pronator drift and mild right-sided weakness (4/5 in right arm, 4+/5 right leg) — subtle, resolving over the exam. Right-sided hyperreflexia with upgoing plantar on the right. No neck stiffness, no papilloedema on fundoscopy (though view partial). Lateral tongue laceration on the right side noted. Cranial nerves otherwise intact.

investigations.name: CT brain with contrast
investigations.result: Multiple (3) ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white junction and left basal ganglia with surrounding vasogenic oedema and mild mass effect; no midline shift

investigations.name: Toxoplasma IgM serology
investigations.result: Negative (consistent with reactivation of latent infection rather than acute primary infection)

investigations.name: Serum lactate (drawn ~30 min post-seizure)
investigations.result: 3.1 mmol/L, trending to normal on repeat at 1 hour — consistent with a true convulsive seizure

investigations.name: FBC, U&E, Ca, Mg, phosphate, LFT
investigations.result: Mild normocytic anaemia (Hb 10.9), electrolytes and renal/liver function normal

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: No infiltrate, no cavitation, no lymphadenopathy

investigations.name: Lumbar puncture
investigations.result: Deferred acutely due to focal deficit and ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect on CT — LP contraindicated until mass lesions have been addressed/re-imaged

investigations.name: EEG
investigations.result: Not performed acutely; would be considered later for classification, not for exclusion of epilepsy

pathophys.focal-onset seizure with secondary gener: Toxoplasma gondii tachyzoites reactivate from latent bradyzoite cysts in the severely immunosuppressed brain (CD4 <100), causing necrotising encephalitis with surrounding vasogenic oedema; the irritable, disorganised cortical focus at the lesion margin generates abnormal electrical discharge that begins focally (right arm) before spreading to involve the whole cortex (secondary generalisation)
pathophys.Todd's paresis / preceding right-sided w: Transient post-ictal neuronal exhaustion and local inhibitory processes in the affected (left hemisphere) cortex produce contralateral weakness that resolves within 48 hours; in this case a structural lesion in the same region also contributes a true focal deficit
pathophys.headache and fever preceding the seizure: Mass effect and oedema from expanding necrotic toxoplasma abscesses raise local and sometimes global intracranial pressure, while cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) from the inflammatory/necrotic process drives fever and headache
pathophys.multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the g: Haematogenous dissemination of reactivated tachyzoites preferentially seeds the richly vascularised grey-white junction and basal ganglia; the enhancing rim represents a zone of inflammatory blood-brain barrier breakdown around central necrosis
pathophys.post-ictal confusion: Neuronal metabolic exhaustion (depleted ATP, accumulated extracellular potassium and adenosine) and ongoing subclinical cortical dysfunction after the seizure's excitation/inhibition imbalance resolves

staging: WHO HIV clinical stage 4 (cerebral toxoplasmosis, an AIDS-defining illness); provoked (acute symptomatic) focal seizure secondary to structural CNS lesion — does not yet meet ILAE unprovoked epilepsy criteria but carries high recurrence risk while the lesion is active

immediate: Protect airway, ensure IV access, correct glucose if needed (already normal here)
If seizure recurs/persists >5 minutes (t1 for GTCS): IV lorazepam or diazepam as first-line status epilepticus treatment
Load with a non-enzyme-inducing antiseizure medication (levetiracetam preferred) given need for future ART/TB drug compatibility
Urgent CT brain with contrast (already performed) — defer lumbar puncture given mass lesions with oedema and focal deficit
Admit for neurological observation and monitoring of GCS/focal signs
definitive: Empirical anti-toxoplasma therapy: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid (leucovorin) for 6 weeks, or co-trimoxazole high-dose as an alternative per SA guidelines

Reassess clinically and radiologically at 2 weeks — expect clinical and radiological improvement with correct diagnosis; failure to improve prompts consideration of biopsy for lymphoma/other pathology
Re-initiate ART (previous regimen review, likely TLD) after a short delay (typically ~2 weeks) once toxoplasmosis treatment established, to reduce risk of IRIS
Continue antiseizure medication — levetiracetam or lamotrigine preferred over enzyme-inducing agents (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone) which will reduce ART levels and vice versa
Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis (already part of/aligned with treatment given CD4 <200)
supportive: Adherence counselling addressing the reasons for prior ART default (relocation, embarrassment) with a treatment supporter and simplified clinic transfer arrangement
Seizure safety advice: avoid swimming alone, avoid operating machinery, driving cessation and document this advice given (SA Road Traffic Act medicolegal requirement)
Counsel regarding risk of IRIS symptoms when ART is reintroduced
Psychosocial support given diagnosis of advanced HIV and disclosure concerns
followUp: Repeat CT/MRI brain at 2 weeks to confirm radiological response to anti-toxoplasma therapy
CD4 and viral load monitoring on ART re-initiation

Neurology/HIV clinic follow-up for antiseizure medication review — reassess need for long-term therapy once the acute provoking lesion has resolved (this was a provoked seizure, not yet epilepsy by ILAE criteria)
Screen for depression and provide adherence support at each visit
Household/contact TB screening not indicated here (GeneXpert negative) but maintain vigilance

stationChecklist.item: Obtains a detailed eyewitness/collateral account (asks for a contact number to phone the witness)
stationChecklist.answer: Sister witnessed right arm jerking, cyanosis, tongue bite, prolonged confusion afterward
stationChecklist.why: The single most valuable investigation in any seizure presentation is an eyewitness account

stationChecklist.item: Characterises the three phases of the event: prodrome/aura, ictal phase, post-ictal phase
stationChecklist.answer: No aura; focal right arm jerking evolving to generalised tonic-clonic activity; 40 minutes of post-ictal confusion
stationChecklist.why: Localises seizure onset (focal-onset with secondary generalisation) and distinguishes from mimics

stationChecklist.item: Actively screens for syncope/PNES discriminators (colour, tongue bite site, recovery speed, triggers)
stationChecklist.answer: Cyanosed (not pale), lateral tongue bite, slow/confused recovery — all favour true seizure over syncope
stationChecklist.why: Seizure vs syncope discrimination is a core exam teaching point

stationChecklist.item: Asks about precipitants and works through provoked vs unprovoked framework (glucose, alcohol, fever, focal symptoms preceding)
stationChecklist.answer: Preceding headache, fever, and progressive right hand clumsiness for a week before the seizure — points to an underlying structural/infective lesion
stationChecklist.why: Provoked vs unprovoked is explicitly flagged as THE key clinical decision determining lifelong medication vs treating the underlying cause

stationChecklist.item: Takes a full HIV history: status, CD4/VL history, ART regimen and adherence, reasons for any default
stationChecklist.answer: HIV positive 6 years, defaulted ART 8 months ago after relocating, embarrassed to seek care
stationChecklist.why: Any new seizure with CD4 <200 needs urgent workup for HIV-related CNS opportunistic disease

stationChecklist.item: Screens for TB contact, cough, night sweats, prior TB treatment
stationChecklist.answer: No TB contact, no cough, no prior TB treatment
stationChecklist.why: TB (tuberculoma/TBM) is a key differential in any HIV-positive patient with a new CNS lesion and must be actively excluded

stationChecklist.item: Performs a focused neurological exam looking for focal deficit, Todd's paresis, meningism, papilloedema
stationChecklist.answer: Right pronator drift, right-sided weakness and hyperreflexia, upgoing right plantar; no neck stiffness
stationChecklist.why: Focal deficit lateralises the lesion and is a red flag mandating urgent imaging before LP

stationChecklist.item: Inspects for lateral tongue laceration and other injury from the convulsion
stationChecklist.answer: Lateral tongue laceration present on the right side
stationChecklist.why: Highly specific sign for a true generalised tonic-clonic seizure versus syncope/PNES

stationChecklist.item: Generates a ranked differential centred on HIV-related CNS mass lesions (toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, lymphoma) with reasoning linked to CD4 and imaging pattern
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning using CD4 count and lesion pattern is the core exam philosophy for this case

stationChecklist.item: Requests urgent CT brain with contrast before considering LP, plus HIV/CD4/VL and Toxoplasma serology
stationChecklist.answer: CT shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions at grey-white junction/basal ganglia; CD4 48; Toxoplasma IgG positive
stationChecklist.why: CT before LP is mandatory with focal signs and possible mass lesion; CD4 and serology confirm the diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Correctly states the status epilepticus t1 timepoint (5 minutes for GTCS) as the threshold to start treating with IV benzodiazepine
stationChecklist.answer: IV lorazepam or diazepam at 5 minutes of continuous or repeated seizure activity without recovery
stationChecklist.why: The t1/t2 status epilepticus timepoints are explicitly emphasised and highly testable

stationChecklist.item: Selects an antiseizure medication that avoids enzyme induction (levetiracetam/lamotrigine/valproate with caution) given ART and future TB treatment interactions
stationChecklist.why: Enzyme-inducing ASMs undermine ART (dolutegravir/efavirenz/PI) and rifampicin — explicitly flagged as a high-yield, locally relevant point

stationChecklist.item: Outlines empirical anti-toxoplasma therapy (pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/folinic acid or co-trimoxazole), timing of ART re-initiation, and safety/driving advice
stationChecklist.answer: 6 weeks anti-toxo therapy, ART restarted after short delay to reduce IRIS risk, driving cessation documented
stationChecklist.why: Complete, guideline-based management including medicolegal seizure safety advice
